title: Fairy Tale Friends
objectives: I can tell about a giant, a castle, and a brave character.
I can tell a wish and what magic could do.
I can use story words to retell or act out a fairy tale.
rationale: Fairy tales are some of the richest read-aloud language in kindergarten, and these five words let children retell and act out the stories they love. Giant and castle name what children picture; brave, wish, and magic name the feelings and powers that move a tale. All five carry over to many books children will meet. The unit closes the year by revisiting character, problem, tall, and worried, because a fairy tale puts a character with a problem in a place and lets a brave choice solve it.

words.def: A very, very big person in a story.
words.ex: The giant stepped over the hill.
words.ex2: The little girl was not afraid of the giant.
words.nonExample: A small mouse is not a giant.

passage.title: Tia and the Giant
paras: Brave Tia lives near a castle. A giant sits by the gate and cries.
He has a problem: everyone is worried and runs away. Tia makes a wish and walks up to him.
Magic sparkles in the air, and the giant smiles. Now he has a new friend.

qs.q: Tia is brave. What does she do?
choices: She walks up to the giant.
qs.why: A brave person does hard things even when scared; Tia walks up to the giant.
His problem is that everyone is worried and runs away.

qs.q: What happens after Tia makes a wish?
choices: The giant smiles and gets a friend.
qs.why: Magic sparkles, and the giant smiles and has a new friend.

write.prompt: Draw yourself being brave, or draw a wish. Tell a partner about your picture.

study.task: Act out each story word: stand tall like a giant, make a wish with your hands, wave a magic wand, and show how a brave person stands.

teacher.overview: Children learn five fairy tale words by acting out a giant, a wish, a wand, and a brave stance, then hear them in a short tale and retell it with the words. Everything is oral and acted; no reading is needed.

notes.va.giant.n: Use a fairy tale picture book and compare a giant with a mouse using hands. Giant here is a noun, a very big person in a story. The adjective giant, as in a giant cake, is not taught. Review tall: how tall is a giant?
notes.va.castle.n: Show pictures of towers, a gate, and a bridge. A castle is a big stone building; children may also know a sand castle, which is a pretend one. Ask who lives in a castle in the stories they know.
notes.va.brave.adj: Brave does not mean not scared. A brave person is scared and still does the hard thing. Review worried by asking how a character feels before a brave act.
notes.va.wish.n: Teach the noun, something you hope for. The verb, as in I wish I could, is not taught. Do not promise that wishes come true; say it is something you hope for.
notes.va.magic.n: Magic here means special powers in stories. Be clear that magic tricks are tricks, and that stories are pretend. The word is common in read-alouds, so name it each time it appears.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'In this story there is a giant by a castle. He has a problem, because everyone runs away. Tia is brave. She is scared, but she walks up to him. She makes a wish. Then there is magic. Let's retell it together.'
discuss: Which character in a fairy tale is brave? What did they do?
What problem could a giant solve if someone was kind to him?
misconceptions: Magic is real in the same way as the weather.
extend: Act out Tia and the Giant as a class play with a pretend castle.
Draw a wish and magic page for a class fairy tale book.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit character and problem by retelling a familiar tale, and tall and worried by describing the giant and the villagers. Use brave, wish, and magic in grade 1 retellings with first, next, and then.

wida.oral: Partner A starts a fairy tale with 'There was a giant by a castle.' Partner B adds one sentence using brave, wish, or magic, and they take turns to finish the tale.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (gigante, castillo, valiente, deseo, magia) have not been reviewed by a native speaker; valiente and bravo both fit brave, and deseo can also mean desire.
Sense boundary: giant is taught as the noun for a very big person in a story; the adjective use (a giant cake) is left out. Wish is taught as a noun only, though the verb is common.
Visual: the giant glyph uses a troll-like emoji that may render differently by platform; check the rendering for fit.
Tier note: all five words are general or Tier 2; castle and giant are story words that are very frequent in K read-alouds.
